blocks.text: My name is Tova Horton. I’m 33, and five Thanksgivings ago, my mother called to tell me not to come home.
“Your sister doesn’t want drama,” she said, and hung up before I could ask what drama.
So I drove into the Kansas prairie and ate turkey alone at a small-town cafe.
The old couple at the next table pulled out a chair for me.
A year before my wedding, that couple became my legal family.
My parents found out at my wedding from a folded paper program in front of 140 guests.
But it wasn’t my new last name that made my father kick a chair across the grass.
The call came at 11:40 on a Monday night in November.
I was 28, three hours into a night shift at the hospital pharmacy in Emporia, checking a nurse’s order for a heparin drip.
My mother never called during my shifts. She said night work was for people who couldn’t find day jobs.
So when her name lit up my phone, I stepped into the hallway thinking somebody had died.
“Tova,” she said, “don’t come home for Thanksgiving this year.”
“Nobody’s sick. Your sister’s fiancé’s family is coming. The Bllelocks. They’re very nice people.”
I asked her what drama she meant, and she said I knew exactly what drama.
I stood in that hallway under the buzzing lights with my phone in my hand and the heparin order in the other.
I’m a pharmacist. I paid for school by working as a pharmacy tech at a grocery store in Wichita, nights and weekends for six years.
I came out of the University of Kansas with a doctorate and $160,000 in loans. And I was paying them down at $1,100 a month.
My job is to read the fine print on other people’s medicine and say no when no is the safe answer.
I went back inside, verified the heparin drip, and finished my shift.
I knew exactly what drama my mother meant.
It had happened in September at the pharmacy counter, and it had a name.
Phyllis Moberly had been my mother’s best friend since their sorority days.
And in September, she came with my mother to the grocery store pharmacy where I still picked up weekend shifts.
My mother leaned over the counter like she was ordering coffee.
“Phyllis ran out of her pain pills. She said her doctor’s in Branson until Tuesday. Just give her a few of mine. You know my prescription.”
She laughed the way she laughs at church when someone’s joke isn’t funny.
Handing a patient’s medication to somebody else is a felony, and it’s the fastest way for a pharmacist to lose her license and land in a courtroom.
I offered to call Phyllis’s doctor’s on-call line. I offered to help her find an urgent care.
She walked out to the parking lot without a word.
And that night, she called and told me I had humiliated her in front of her oldest friend.
“You made me look like a criminal,” she said.
I said I was trying to keep everyone from becoming one.
“That’s exactly what I mean,” she said. “You always have to make everything a production.”
By October, my mother had a word for me, and she used it with everybody.
And my sister Chelsea, who had just gotten engaged, heard it, too.
And difficult in my mother’s house was the first cousin of drama.
The next afternoon, I called my mother back and asked to speak to Chelsea.
“She’s busy,” my mother said. “Don’t make this worse.”
I asked for Chelsea’s new number because she’d changed it after the engagement, and I’d only found out when my texts went green.
“I’m not giving you her number so you can upset her,” my mother said.
My father got on the line just long enough to say, “Listen to your mother.”
My mother was the only door to my sister, and she had locked it from the inside.
So on Thanksgiving morning, I woke up in my apartment in Emporia with nowhere to be.
The neighbor’s TV was already playing the parade through the wall.
I put on my thickest green cardigan, got in my little Honda, and drove west into the Flint Hills with no plan at all.
If you’ve never seen the Flint Hills in late November, it’s a sea of tall grass gone the color of a lion, rolling under a huge pale sky.
With barbed-wire fences and limestone posts running off to nowhere, the wind pushes the grass in long waves.
It’s the loneliest, loveliest place in Kansas.
Thirty-five minutes later, I came over a rise into a town called Elm Creek, population 400 and some, and saw a chalkboard sign outside a brick building on the main street.
Then I went inside because I figured I counted as a stray.
The Junction Cafe had a pressed-tin ceiling, a long Formica counter, and eight booths along the windows.
It smelled like sage stuffing and burnt coffee.
There were maybe 20 people inside, mostly older men in seed caps eating alone, a few truckers, and one table of four teenagers in 4-H jackets.
A woman with silver braids and an apron that said “Bonnie” took my money and pointed me to the buffet.
I filled a plate and sat in a booth by the window.
And by the time I’d finished checking my phone for a message that never came, the gravy had gone cold.
The man was tall, maybe 65, with a sunburned neck and big ranch hands, and he was cutting his wife’s turkey into small squares because her right wrist was in a cast.
She was small and sharp-eyed, with short white hair and reading glasses on a beaded chain.
